title: Export step: regenerate meanings.json from the lexicon DB
description:
DECISIONS.md D1 commits to keeping the runtime on data/meanings.json while the lexicon SQLite DB serves as the authoring-side store (mining, citation tracking, consensus, lemma linkage). The decision says 'a future export step (filed) will regenerate meanings.json from the lexicon when we want changes to ship.' That export step is not actually filed anywhere I can find — no ticket, no script, no module. This issue covers building it.

Scope:
- A CLI command (likely 'wyrd kenning export-meanings' or similar) that walks the lexicon DB, applies the promotion criteria, and writes a fresh meanings.json + the four <culture>_proportions.json files used by the runtime.
- Promotion criteria per D4: include etymons with N>=3 distinct scholar-witness citations and no breakdown disagreement. Etymons still standing on rando-port (Wikipedia seed) alone are included as legacy until corroborated.
- Per D14, hedged extractions (confidence='low') are exported but tagged so consumers can filter.
- Per D8, lemma+inflection linkage means we export the lemma's surface form with a side-table or inline note for inflected variants (whichever the runtime can consume without a refactor).
- Per D18, attested spelling variants (etymon_text_match.matched_form) ship alongside the canonical form so the generator can sample them — coordinate with wyrd-40m.
- Per D12, do NOT export search-evidence (etymon_text_match) as if it were citation evidence; only etymon_citation rolls up to consensus.

Acceptance:
- Re-running the export against the current lexicon produces a meanings.json that the existing kenning generator and KenningExplain explainer can load without changes.
- All existing tests still pass against the regenerated file.
- The exported file's morpheme count is >= the current bundled meanings.json (no regressions from the rando-port seed).
- Diff between regenerated and current bundled meanings.json is reviewable and surfaces the actual newly-promoted etymons.

Why this is load-bearing: every mining ticket (wyrd-yy3, wyrd-bzu, wyrd-gxf, wyrd-zga, wyrd-9w8, wyrd-3qq, wyrd-i88, wyrd-95f, the Mayan/Nahuatl ones, and wyrd-668) is currently queued behind this. Without the export, mining accrues to the lexicon but never reaches the user.

title: Parallelize LLM mining loop in lexicon_mine_llm
description:
gemini-code-assist (PR #3 round 2, P1) flagged: `lexicon_mine_llm` processes entries sequentially with one network request per entry. For large books this is slow.

Proposal: `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` to fire several extract_one calls in parallel, with rate-limit awareness for paid providers (Anthropic/Gemini have request-per-minute caps).

Caveats to think through:
- Ollama on a single GPU host serializes anyway — concurrency lift is mostly relevant for paid providers.
- Anthropic/Gemini rate limits: need a simple semaphore plus retry-with-backoff on 429.
- Existing per-entry log line and incremental DB write would need to be ordered or labeled to stay legible.
- The validation guard (D3) must remain per-entry; no batched validation.

Out-of-scope marker per PR #3 review.

title: Use attested spelling variants as randomizer targets in generation
description:
Per user observation: 19th-c scholars wrote 'denu' / 'dene' / 'denū' / 'dená' for the same OE word — spelling wasn't standardized. With the gloss-anchored fuzzy match work (etymon_text_match.matched_form), we now know each etymon's attested spelling variants across the corpus.

This is a generative feature, not just verification. When the kenning generator picks a morpheme, instead of always emitting the canonical form, it can RANDOMLY SAMPLE from the attested spellings:

  Pick etymon: 'denu' (OE valley)
  Attested variants: denu (8×), dene (12×), denū (3×), dená (1×)
  Sample weighted by attestation count → emit one of these in the output

Effect on output quality:
- Names feel pulled from real period documents instead of a database
- Different invocations produce stylistically varied output even with the same morpheme set
- For historical-mode generation (era=Old English), the variant feels more authentic
- For modern-mode generation, we use the canonical / modernized form

Implementation:
- Each etymon already has a canonical_form. The attested variants live in etymon_text_match.matched_form (after the fuzzy-search work).
- Add a function get_attested_variants(etymon_id) -> [(form, count), ...]
- Generation step that currently emits etymon.canonical_form → instead samples from variants weighted by count, with the canonical form having a baseline weight to ensure it shows up.
- A user-facing --variant-style flag: 'canonical' (current behavior, always canonical), 'attested' (sample from variants), 'random' (uniform over variants).

Pairs with wyrd-skm (period-aware) — different variants are more/less period-appropriate, and the generator should weight by period when emitting.

title: Capture attribution snippets for in-app citation display
description:
Currently when an etymon has a citation, we record source_id + page (mostly null) + short_quote (sometimes set). For end-users to see WHY they should trust an etymology, we should capture the surrounding text context so the app can show:

  hām (Old English, 'home/settlement')
    cited by: Mawer 1920, Northumberland and Durham
    in entry: 'Acklington (Warkworth). 1176 Pipe Eclinton... O.E. Æcceling(a)tun
              = farm of Æccel or of his sons.'
    cited by: Skeat 1901, Cambridgeshire
    in entry: 'Hadenham. ...A.S. Hædan-ham, Kemble, Cod. Dipl. vi. 98...
              Here ham is "home."'

Implementation:
1. For LLM-extracted citations, store the entry's body text (or a configurable-length snippet) as the citation context. Currently we store ~200 chars in source_quote — bump to 500+ for richer display.
2. For reverse-search citations (wyrd-bgr-style), capture ±100 chars around each match position.
3. Add etymon_citation.context_snippet TEXT column (or reuse short_quote with a longer length budget).
4. Page numbers: parse from the OCR text where possible (running headers like 'CAMBRIDGESHIRE 47' appear consistently in Skeat). Add etymon_citation.page when extractable.
5. App display: when user clicks an etymon, show all citations with context. Optionally render the surrounding sentence as a tooltip / expansion.

Pairs with the runtime LLM features (wyrd-e67) — Bedrock could synthesize 'why this etymology is reasonable' explanations from the raw scholar quotes.

This makes the lexicon a teaching tool, not just a generation backend. A user playing with the SPA can see WHY the engine thinks 'Bridg-' is a real morpheme — because three published scholars wrote the following passages...

title: MCP server: expose wyrd APIs to GMs via Claude / other AI assistants
description:
Wrap the wyrd HTTP API (or core generation functions directly) as an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server so GMs can use Claude / Cursor / other AI assistants to call the generator with rich natural-language constraints.

Use case: GM says to Claude 'give me 10 names for villages in a Norse-influenced coastal region in the 12th century, all with water-related morphemes, presented as a markdown table with pronunciation guides.' Claude calls wyrd's MCP tools to actually generate, then formats as requested.

Tools to expose:
- generate(culture, era, register, tags, count, novelty, seed) → list of structured names with breakdowns
- explain(name) → morpheme decomposition with all matching readings
- convert(name, target_register) → cross-register rendering (when wyrd-4cd ships)
- pronounce(name, language) → respelling + IPA
- lexicon_search(form_or_gloss) → all etymons matching, with citations
- list_pantheons() / get_deity(pantheon, name) → for deity-based naming
- pin_name(name, target_register) → conjugate user-supplied name into register

Architecture options:
1. Python MCP server using the official Python SDK, calls into wyrd's existing generate/explain functions directly (no HTTP). Cleanest for a single-machine GM.
2. HTTP-fronting MCP server that calls the deployed lambda. Useful for multi-user setups.
3. Both (start with 1, add 2 if there's demand).

Distribution: package as 'wyrd-mcp' with an entry point in pyproject.toml, then a GM does:
  pip install wyrd-mcp
  # add to ~/.config/Claude/mcp_servers.json
  # restart Claude
  # GM types: 'generate me 5 elven villages in the Shire'

Killer feature: GM gets fluent natural-language access to a constrained, reproducible generator — Claude handles the parsing of intent, wyrd handles the constrained generation. Better than either alone.

title: Mine French place-name etymology corpora
description:
Per Claude-twin feedback. Standard reference is Dauzat's Dictionnaire étymologique des noms de lieux en France (not PD). PD options:

- Auguste Longnon, 'Les Noms de lieu de la France: Leur origine, leur signification, leurs transformations' (1920-29) — published right at our PD cutoff, foundational.
- Jules Quicherat, 'De la formation française des anciens noms de lieu' (1867) — earlier PD, good for the older strata (Frankish, Gallo-Roman).
- Egloff Fluck, 'Toponymie française' — early 1900s
- Various per-region French toponymy gazetteers from 1880-1920

French as a fantasy register codes 'Norman noble', 'Frankish substrate', 'Gallo-Roman bones' — three strata corresponding to wyrd-{stratification} once that's filed. Mining these gives the morpheme inventory.

Pairs with the manorial-affix pattern (wyrd-{manorial}) — Norman family names extracted from this corpus + Domesday tenant lists make the conquest-layering generation viable.

title: Within-language stratum tagging (Brittonic/Latin/medieval/English in 'Welsh')
description:
Each major language palette has internal stratification we currently ignore:

- Welsh: Brittonic substrate + Latin layer (caer, pont, ffynnon — direct Latin loans) + native medieval Welsh + English borrowings + modern. A 'Welsh-flavored elven' generator pulling indiscriminately from all of it produces stylistic mush.
- French: Frankish substrate (-ville, -court, personal names in -hard / -old) + Gallo-Roman + medieval French + early modern + Occitan-influenced south.
- Old English: West Saxon vs Mercian vs Anglian dialect strata; pre-Christian vs Christian-influenced vocabulary.
- Old Norse: Eastern (Swedish/Danish) vs Western (Norwegian/Icelandic) traditions.

Schema addition: 'stratum' text column on etymon (or a separate etymon_stratum table for many-to-many — a morpheme can belong to multiple strata as it crosses periods).

Generation gains a --stratum filter:
  --style elven --stratum brittonic       → pre-Latin-influence Welsh-coded names
  --style elven --stratum medieval-welsh  → high-medieval flavor
  --style noble --stratum frankish        → 'pre-Gallo-Roman' French
  --style noble --stratum high-medieval   → standard chivalric French

Within-language stratum is the missing axis to sit alongside the cross-language wyrd-sfp work and the time-period wyrd-skm work.

title: Probabilistic morpheme co-occurrence learned from corpus
description:
Instead of hand-coding selectional restrictions on which morphemes combine with which (wyrd-{selection-restrictions}), build a co-occurrence matrix from the existing corpus and sample from the empirical distribution.

For each generic (-tun, -ham, -by, -worth, -ham, etc.), record the distribution of first-elements that ACTUALLY appear with it across attested toponyms, weighted by frequency.

Generation:
1. Pick a generic according to the language's structural pattern.
2. Sample a first-element from that generic's empirical co-occurrence distribution rather than uniformly from all etymons.

Wins:
- Catches implicit selectional restrictions WITHOUT having to hand-encode them.
- Surfaces regional patterns automatically (-thorpe concentrates with certain personal-name types in certain Yorkshire ridings; -by has a Danelaw signature; -wick fades after 1100). These show up in the matrix even if we never noticed them.
- Frequency-weighted: morphemes that are productive get used more, dead-ends get used less.
- Empirically grounded: the generator imitates real attested patterns rather than reasoning about them.

Implementation:
- New view or precomputed table: cooccurrence (first_etymon_id, second_etymon_id, count, weighted_count_by_period_and_region).
- Update NameGenerator.select() in proportions.py to consult cooccurrence stats when picking the second element given the first.
- Optional --no-cooccurrence flag for diagnostic comparison vs uniform sampling.

This basically obviates a large chunk of wyrd-{selection-restrictions} for free, and the test is concrete: generate 100 names with cooccurrence on, 100 with it off, eyeball both. The cooccurrence ones should read meaningfully more plausible.

Probably one of the highest-value tickets in the queue for output quality with little incremental work.
notes:
CORRECTION: marginal frequency-weighting is ALREADY in Rando (now wyrd) via proportions.py — usages and structures tables count how often each morpheme and each structural shape appears in real place names, and NameGenerator samples accordingly.

What's NOT in Rando is the CONDITIONAL joint distribution. The current generator samples each compound slot independently of the others — pick a -tun weighted by marginal -tun frequency, then independently pick a first-element by marginal frequency. There's no 'given that post-element is -tun, what's the distribution of typical pre-elements?'

The actual upgrade is adding the joint:
  P(first | second)
in addition to the existing marginal:
  P(first), P(second)

This catches the missing piece — that real corpora have strong selectional preferences (-tun pairs with personal-name and topographic prefixes; -ingaham pairs differently; -thorpe has Yorkshire personal-name regional bias). Independent sampling produces marginal-correct but joint-wrong combinations.

So this ticket is incremental on top of Rando's frequency-weighting, not a wholesale change. The data structure addition is one new precomputed table:
  cooccurrence (slot_a_etymon_id, slot_b_etymon_id, count)
The generation change is in proportions.py NameGenerator: sample slot 2 conditionally on slot 1 instead of independently. ~30 lines of Python.

Lower-effort than I initially framed it. Still high-value because joint vs marginal is what makes the difference between 'plausible morphology' and 'plausible attested name'.
REFINEMENT (per user, conversation): pure empirical co-occurrence has a known failure mode — it can only generate combinations that ALREADY appeared in the corpus. For a fantasy name generator we explicitly want NOVEL plausible names, not corpus retrieval.

Fix: Bayesian mixture model rather than pure empirical sampling.

  P(slot_b | slot_a) = α · P_empirical(slot_b | slot_a)        # attested co-occurrence
                     + β · P_class(slot_b | type(slot_a))       # selectional-type backoff
                     + γ · P_marginal(slot_b)                    # current Rando independent

with α + β + γ = 1.

Three regimes:
- α dominant: conservative, 'only attested combinations'. Good for testing, bad for generation.
- β dominant: feature-class backoff via selectional types (personal-name, topographic, ethnic-name, etc — same tags as wyrd-r8b). Generates NOVEL combinations within observed type patterns. Probably the sweet spot for fantasy-naming.
- γ dominant: reverts to current Rando behavior (independent marginals). Max novelty.

User-facing --novelty parameter lets a GM choose where to sit:
  --novelty conservative   → α=0.7, β=0.25, γ=0.05  (mostly attested)
  --novelty plausible      → α=0.3, β=0.55, γ=0.15  (default, type-driven novelty)
  --novelty wild           → α=0.1, β=0.3,  γ=0.6   (mostly marginal)

Smoothing: Laplace (add-1 to all pairs) or Kneser-Ney are standard NLP techniques, both short Python implementations. Required so unseen pairs get non-zero probability.

The β term depends on selectional types being tagged on etymons — that's wyrd-r8b. So sequence is:
  1. wyrd-r8b: tag etymons with selectional types (personal-name / topographic / etc.)
  2. wyrd-mj2 (this): build co-occurrence + class-level distributions
  3. Wire into NameGenerator with --novelty knob

Generation quality vs novelty becomes a tunable tradeoff, not a binary.
REFRAMED (per user): co-occurrence should operate on SEMANTIC CATEGORIES (tags), not morpheme IDs. The existing etymon_tag table already has these — plant, tree, water, religion, food, architecture, directional, male/female/saint name, etc.

Why semantic-class is the right level:

1. SPARSITY: ~30-50 tag classes vs ~2000 morpheme IDs. K×K matrix has ~1500 cells with hundreds of pairs each, vs N×N with most empty. The model actually fits the data.

2. GENERALIZATION: once we learn 'TREE + COLOR' pairs commonly, EVERY (oak, green) / (birch, white) / (ash, grey) is plausible whether attested or not. Solves the 'novel combinations from sparse data' problem.

3. CROSS-LANGUAGE: 'trees pair with greens' works in Welsh and Latin the same as in OE. wyrd-sfp (cross-cultural rendering) gets free transfer — semantic categories are language-neutral.

4. GM USABILITY: GM thinking 'forest village' picks (TREE + SETTLEMENT) tags; engine fills morphemes. Much better interface than picking morpheme IDs.

Revised generation flow:

  1. Pick structural pattern (1-word / 2-word / compound) — already in Rando.
  2. For each slot, sample a SEMANTIC CATEGORY using tag-level Bayesian
     conditional model:
       P(tag_b | tag_a) = α · P_empirical(tag_b | tag_a)
                        + β · P_marginal(tag_b)
     (Two-term mixture is sufficient at the tag level; the K×K matrix
     is dense enough that we don't need a third feature-backoff term.)
  3. For each picked category, sample a specific morpheme within that
     category, weighted by morpheme-marginal frequency PLUS stratum/
     period/region filters.
  4. Apply per-language mutation/sandhi (wyrd-q5v).

Morpheme-level conditional-frequency P(morpheme_b | morpheme_a) becomes a refinement, not the core. Most of the linguistic plausibility lives at the tag level.

Implementation: precompute a tag_cooccurrence table from existing toponym_etymology_element joins. Update NameGenerator.select() to do the two-stage sample. ~50 lines of Python plus a small precompute script.

Concrete next steps:
  1. wyrd-r8b (selectional types) is partially redundant now — modifier_tags already serve as semantic-type labels for most cases. Possibly close r8b in favor of fully leveraging existing tags.
  2. Build the tag_cooccurrence table.
  3. Wire two-stage sampling into NameGenerator.
  4. Generate 100 names with --novelty=plausible, eyeball, compare to current marginal-only sampling.
FITNESS TEST (per user, conversation): Rando produced 'Braitham Gate' — a felicitous novel name combining Brait- (size/broad) + -ham (habitative) + Gate (boundary/infrastructure). None of those exact morpheme combinations were attested as a real place in the corpus, but the tag-pattern structure they instantiate was attested hundreds of times.

This is the exact scenario the tag-level co-occurrence approach handles well that morpheme-level co-occurrence would have killed:

- Morpheme-level: P(Brait-, -ham) ≈ 0 (never attested as a specific pair). P(Braitham, Gate) = 0. Kills the output.
- Tag-level: P(size, habitative) for word-1 internal compound is high. P(habitative, boundary/infrastructure) for word-2 follow-up is moderate. Both supported by hundreds of attested toponyms (Long-X-Gate, Great-X-Bridge, Broad-X-Cross). The novel combination of specific morphemes within those classes is exactly what we want.

Adding a regression test as part of this ticket's acceptance criteria:

  def test_generator_still_produces_braitham_gate_shaped_names():
      '''Rando produced this; the new architecture must not lose the
      capability for this kind of novel-yet-plausible combination.'''
      samples = [generate() for _ in range(5000)]
      matching = [
          s for s in samples
          if has_pattern(s, words=2,
                         word1_tags=(('size','descriptive'), ('habitative',)),
                         word2_tags=('boundary','infrastructure'))
      ]
      assert len(matching) > 5  # rare but should fire

This is the load-bearing test that prevents the sophisticated probabilistic model from accidentally narrowing the output distribution to only-attested-shapes. The novelty-knob (α/β mixture) needs to stay loose enough that this test passes at the default setting.

title: Norman+English manorial-affix layering as a generation pattern
description:
A specific compositional pattern that English place naming captures densely: English/ON base name + French manorial affix marking the lord's family. Captures the political history of conquest layering directly in the toponym.

Real examples (Domesday and post-Conquest):
- Stoke Mandeville (English Stoke + Norman Mandeville family)
- Ashby de la Zouch (ON Ashby + Norman La Zouche family)
- Newton Poppleford (English Newton + Norman Poppleford family)
- Stanton Lacy (English Stanton + Norman Lacy family)
- Castle Cary (English Castle + Norman Cary family)

As a generation pattern: pick any English/ON base toponym, attach a Norman manorial affix from a sampled noble family. Output reads as 'a town that was conquered and now bears its conqueror's family name' — gameable settlement-name structure encoding political history.

Implementation: needs (a) a corpus of Norman manorial families (extractable from Domesday + later subsidy rolls — many in PD scholarly compilations), (b) a generation mode where a base name is paired with an affix from this corpus.

Killer for fantasy worldbuilding: the GM picks 'this region was conquered 200 years ago by House Mortemer' and the generator produces a region of base names with Mortemer affixes ('Hadenham Mortemer', 'Crowley Mortemer', etc.). Settlement-name pattern explicitly encodes the political history.

title: Selectional restrictions on etymon co-occurrence
description:
Place-name morphemes aren't freely combinable. -by (ON 'farm/settlement') composes with personal names and topographic features but NOT with other settlement generics. -ham and -tūn both 'farm/settlement' but they have different productive periods and pair with different typical first-elements (Ekwall's introduction details this).

Currently the schema lets the generator combine any first-element with any post-element. That'd produce 'Brycgham' (bridge + home), which never occurs in real corpus and reads as wrong even if morphologically possible.

Schema addition: per-etymon tag column or a new selection_restrictions table:
  etymon_selection (
    etymon_id,
    can_compose_with TEXT,  -- 'personal-name', 'topographic', 'patronymic-ing', etc.
    role TEXT               -- 'as-first-element', 'as-second-element'
  )

Generation samples only morpheme pairs whose selection restrictions are compatible.

This can be hand-coded from Ekwall/Mawer's introductions OR learned probabilistically from the corpus (see wyrd-{co-occurrence ticket}).
notes:
Possibly redundant per user reframing of wyrd-mj2: the existing modifier_tags / etymon_tag system already provides semantic-class labels for most cases (plant, tree, water, religion, architecture, male/female/saint name, directional, size, etc.). The 'selectional restrictions' that wyrd-r8b proposed to encode by hand are largely capturable by tag-level co-occurrence learned from the corpus.

Defer until wyrd-mj2 ships and we see whether the tag-level model captures the selectional patterns adequately. If it does (likely), close r8b. If specific selectional facts persist that tags can't capture (e.g. 'this morpheme only takes patronymics, never personal names' — same tag, different sub-class), then revisit.

title: Phonological mutation / sandhi as post-composition layer
description:
When the generator assembles a name from morphemes, language-specific phonological rules need to apply at the composition boundary. Without these, output reads as wrong-language to native readers (and even non-native readers parse it as 'artificial' without articulating why).

Languages requiring mutation/sandhi rules at composition time:
- Welsh: soft mutation (Caer + Dyfn → Caerddyfn / Caerddyfnaint or whatever the actual rule produces), nasal mutation, aspirate mutation. Mutation depends on the grammatical relation between the two morphemes (genitive, possessive, modifier).
- Old Irish: lenition, eclipsis. Triggered by similar grammatical contexts.
- French: liaison and elision (le + arbre → l'arbre, Saint + Étienne → Saint-Étienne).
- Old English: i-mutation in some compound formations; assimilation rules at consonant-cluster boundaries.

Architecture: a per-language composition_rule function that takes (left-morpheme, right-morpheme, relation) and produces the surface compound. Stored as a Python module per language (welsh_mutation.py, oldirish_mutation.py, etc.) since the rules are linguistic data, not lexicon data.

Critical for the elven=Welsh, noble=French, common=OE registers to feel right. Without it, generated 'Welsh' names will look obviously synthesized to anyone who knows Welsh.

Pairs with wyrd-q5v (composition patterns) — the patterns specify SHAPE, this specifies the phonological glue between slots.

title: Regression-prevention: hedged etymology extraction in SYSTEM_PROMPT
description:
Per user direction (this conversation): scholars frequently hedge etymologies ('perhaps from', 'possibly', 'I only make a guess'). The previous SYSTEM_PROMPT instructed the LLM to set found=false for any case where the scholar 'declines.' This conflated two different failure modes:

  (a) Scholar provides NO etymological claim (cross-reference, attestation list, 'meaning unknown')
  (b) Scholar provides a HEDGED etymology

The previous prompt declined on both, losing all the (b) data. Per Skeat alone, 30-50% of declines are likely hedged etymologies we should be capturing.

Updated SYSTEM_PROMPT to distinguish these. Hedged etymologies now extract with confidence='low' and the hedge phrase in notes. Test case verified on Caxton (Skeat: 'I only make a guess when suggesting...'):
- Old prompt: declined (data lost)
- New prompt: extracted 'Cages' as the genitive prefix, conf='low', notes captures the hedge

Regression-prevention test added in test_kenning_llm_extractor.py: test_system_prompt_distinguishes_hedge_from_no_claim. Asserts the prompt contains 'perhaps', 'hedge', confidence=low, 'no etymological claim', and 'still useful'.

FOLLOW-UP work this enables (filed elsewhere):
- wyrd-bgr: extending the review pipeline to re-process Tier 1 declines now that we know many were hedged-etymology false-declines.
- Re-mining: running Mawer/Skeats with the new prompt would recover the ~120-200 hedged toponyms currently in the 'declined' bucket.

title: Architectural gap: Tier-2 review never sees Tier-1 declines
description:
Identified during Watson investigation. Current review pipeline has a structural blind spot:

- Tier 1 (Qwen) processes every entry. Output is one of: accepted-with-elements (writes toponym_etymology row), declined (writes only a toponym row, no etymology), rejected (writes nothing).
- Tier 2 (Gemini review) only queries toponym_etymology rows tagged as Qwen-extracted with low/medium confidence.

Result: Qwen-DECLINED entries are never re-examined by Gemini or any later tier. If Qwen wrongly declined (which it demonstrably does — see Watson where it declined 95% of Celtic etymology entries that Haiku extracts cleanly from), that data is permanently lost.

Estimated invisible material based on Watson finding (Qwen 3.4% accept vs Haiku ~22%):
- Mawer: 394 declines × likely 30%+ recoverable = ~120 toponyms with hidden etymology
- Watson 1904: ~362 declines × likely 60%+ recoverable = ~200+ toponyms (the Celtic case is extreme)
- Across all Celtic books we'd mine the same way

PROPOSED FIX: extend lexicon review to support a 'declines' mode that picks up toponyms where:
- A toponym row exists for a book
- Either no toponym_etymology row exists, OR the latest one is low-confidence with no elements
- AND no row tagged with the target review-provider exists

Then layered review naturally catches gaps:
  wyrd kenning lexicon review sources/ --mode declines --provider haiku
  → re-extracts what Qwen missed using a stronger Tier 1 candidate

Quick-validation path before building the architectural fix: run Haiku on 50 of Mawer's Qwen-declined toponyms, measure recovery rate. If Haiku extracts from >30% of those, that confirms the gap is real and motivates the architectural change.

title: Empirical finding: Sonnet doesn't lift over Gemini on etymology mining
description:
Tested Anthropic Sonnet 4.6 as a third-tier review provider on Mawer disagreement cases (where Qwen and Gemini gave different breakdowns). Result: Sonnet added noise rather than signal.

SAMPLE (5 disagreement cases, Mawer Northumberland-Durham):
- Allen: Sonnet matched Gemini (tie)
- Angerton: Sonnet hallucinated +tun post-element (Mawer never compounds it). REJECTED by validator.
- Ardley: Sonnet over-canonicalized 'leak' (Mawer's older spelling) to 'leah'. REJECTED.
- Backworth: Sonnet invented a personal-name compound (bacca+worð) when Mawer explicitly hedges the etymology and says it might be named after a school. REJECTED.
- Bagraw: Sonnet matched Gemini (tie).

Net: 0 wins, 3 losses (validator-rejected hallucinations), 2 ties. Cost: ~5 cents.

Plus: there's no 'Gemini-declined' cohort to test Sonnet's rescue capability on Mawer — Gemini accepted all 98 reviewed entries.

INTERPRETATION: Gemini Flash's 'extract only what the text claims' calibration is BETTER matched to etymology mining than Sonnet's 'smart-extrapolation-beyond-the-text' instinct. For this task, source fidelity > inference quality. Sonnet's strength becomes a liability against a strict form-in-body validator (which is what we want).

DECISION:
- Keep the Anthropic provider code (anthropic_extractor.py, --provider anthropic in CLI). Built, tested, idempotent. Available if calibration thinking changes or for different tasks.
- DO NOT run a Sonnet review pass on existing mined data. Negative ROI.
- Reserve Anthropic API budget for user-facing runtime features (wyrd-e67 Bedrock-style use cases) where smart extrapolation is the bottleneck: 'describe this name's setting', 'translate this homebrew deity', 'generate name variations in the same style'.

Future revisit conditions: if we find a class of entries where Gemini consistently fails (e.g. very obscure Celtic books with non-standard formatting), or if we encounter a corpus with very different characteristics (Mesoamerican, Asian languages), Sonnet may add lift there.

title: Body-signal regex too narrow — Celtic / Gaelic books under-yield
description:
The dictionary parser's body-signal validator (added in wyrd-u32) recognizes English-etymology markers (O.E., A.S., O.N., A.F., M.E., year, Phonology) but doesn't include Celtic markers (G., Ir., W., Corn., Brit., Gael.). As a result, Gaelic-language books drop catastrophically:

- Gillies Argyll: 155 → 41 entries
- Johnston Scotland 1892: 2 entries (was higher before)
- Moore Isle of Man: 3 entries (was higher before)

The fix is to broaden _ENTRY_BODY_SIGNALS to include single-letter language abbreviations:
  | G\. | Ir\. | W\. | Corn\. | Brit\. | Gael(?:ic)? | Old\s+Ir(?:ish)? | Welsh

Plus probably: the 'from <foreign-word>' or '<word> = <gloss>' equation patterns common in Celtic etymology books.

Test against Gillies and Watson 1926 to verify the broadened signals catch real Celtic entries without re-introducing the Mawer false-positives that wyrd-u32 fixed.

Lower priority but blocks mining of the Celtic-register sources we'd want for elven/old-folk register densification.
notes:
Related: this also explains why Qwen 9B is declining ~93% of Watson's Ross-and-Cromarty entries (13 accepted out of 240+ at the time of writing). Qwen 9B is English-trained — it sees Watson's Gaelic etymology with G./Ir./W. markers and lacks the English-etymology markers (O.E./A.S.) that anchor its understanding, so it declines.

This makes Watson and other Celtic books exactly the cohort where the layered review (Gemini → Sonnet) might pay off MORE than on English-etymology books like Mawer. Stronger multilingual models would have less English-bias.

Proposed test once Watson Qwen mining finishes: re-mine Watson with --provider gemini (full re-mine, not review), compare accept rate to Qwen's. If Gemini gets >40%, the layered strategy is validated for Celtic corpora and worth running across Joyce, Macbain, Gillies, Watson 1926, etc.
Empirical confirmation in progress: Haiku 4.5 running on Watson 1904 in parallel with Qwen. After 130/380 entries, Haiku has 28 accepted vs Qwen's 13 across the full 380 (final). Haiku's per-entry rate ~22% vs Qwen's 3.4%. ~6× lift from switching Tier 1 from Qwen to Haiku for Celtic content. Total Haiku cost projected at ~$0.50 for the full Watson book.

title: European place-name mining: all the languages with credible PD sources
description:
Mine the major European language families that have credible pre-1929 toponymic scholarship, treating all as morally-neutral palette options for fantasy worldbuilding. The 'dark/menacing' coding is a SEPARATE orthogonal layer (harsh-phonology + grim-semantic-tag filters) that applies to any language. No language is pre-positioned as the bad-guy register.

Languages with good PD source coverage:
- German: Ernst Förstemann, 'Altdeutsches Namenbuch' (1856-), foundational. August Pott, 'Die Personennamen' (1859). Solid PD.
- Italian: Dante Olivieri, Francesco D'Ovidio — early 1900s
- Iberian (Spanish/Portuguese): Madoz's 'Diccionario geográfico-estadístico-histórico de España' (1845-50, very PD); Leite de Vasconcelos for Portuguese
- Slavic (already filed wyrd-i88): Miklosich, Brückner — see that ticket
- Hungarian / Finnish (Uralic): scrappier PD coverage, Hunfalvy late 1800s
- Basque (pre-IE European): Resurrección María de Azkue's dictionary (early 1900s)
- Romanian: Romance + Slavic + Dacian substrate; some early-1900s scholarship
- Greek (already filed wyrd-tqj): Pape, Smith
- Albanian: very limited
- Celtic, Norse, OE, Norman-French, Latin, Welsh: already in our corpus

Each new register adds a distinct fantasy-worldbuilding option:
- German   → Black Forest / mittelmark / pastoral mountain settings
- Italian  → Renaissance city-states / Mediterranean trade
- Spanish  → Iberian frontier / colonial / Reconquista
- Hungarian → Carpathian / steppe-edge
- Finnish  → frozen north / shamanic
- Basque   → ancient pre-IE mystery (genuinely no relatives — a real ethnolinguistic isolate)
- Romanian → Balkan / Dacian-tinted

None is pre-coded for fantasy role. The orthogonal filters (--harsh, --grim, --pastoral, --noble, --imperial) compose with any of these to produce specific moods.

Mining priority order (estimating yield/effort): German > Italian > Spanish > Hungarian > Basque > others.

title: Slavic register for orcish/underdark/foreign-menacing flavor
description:
Slavic fills a specific niche in fantasy register: 'foreign here-and-now-other' rather than 'lost ancient' (substrate) or 'harsh-mountain' (Norse). Tolkien's Black Speech is Slavic-tinted on purpose; fantasy genre has inherited the Slavic-as-menacing convention via D&D's Drow language and decades of pulp novels.

Distinctive markers (what makes Slavic READ slavic to English ears):
- Consonant clusters English doesn't use: Wrocław, Szczecin, Brzeszcze, mst-, pszcz-, vstr-
- /x/ phoneme (Cyrillic Х, Polish ch, transliterated kh) — harsh, no English equivalent
- Final-syllable stress contrasting with English's penult/initial preference
- Distinctive suffixes: -grad (fortress-city), -gorod, -sk, -ovsk, -yn, -ov/-ev/-ow, -ka

Mythology layer (rich material for underdark/dark-fantasy):
- Veles (god of the underworld and cattle), Nav (the dead), Mokosh, Chernobog
- Folk tales: Koschei the Deathless, Baba Yaga, vodyanoy, leshy, rusalka
- Distinct from Norse-mythological or Celtic-fae figures — a separate dark-magic register

PD source coverage (thinner than British-isles but workable):
- Franz Miklosich, 'Die slavischen Ortsnamen aus Appellativen' (1872-74) — foundational comparative Slavic toponymy
- Aleksander Brückner, Słownik etymologiczny języka polskiego (1927) — barely pre-1929
- Various late-1800s per-country gazetteers (Russian, Czech, Polish)

Suggested language tags:
- slavic-east   (Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian)
- slavic-west   (Polish, Czech, Slovak)
- slavic-south  (Serbian-Croatian, Bulgarian, Macedonian)
- Aggregate parent: slavic-family

Combines with the orcish/darklands register from wyrd-{filed earlier}: --style orcish + --slavic-flavor or --style underdark.

SENSITIVITY: Coding 'Slavic = orc' is a recognizable fantasy convention but it's also Cold War-residue xenophobia. Real Slavic peoples are not orcs. Bundle the data, document the connotations honestly, make Slavic ONE option among several for the dark register (not the default). Same posture as for Indigenous languages in wyrd-668.
notes:
REFRAMED per user: do NOT pre-position Slavic as 'orcish/dark.' Slavic is its own register, equally available for noble/heroic/everyday/menacing — the GM decides at use time, not the engine.

Title rename intent: 'Slavic place-name register for fantasy worldbuilding' (drop the orc/underdark coding).

The 'dark/menacing' effect is a SEPARATE orthogonal layer:
- Phonological skew filter (--harsh): prefer harsh consonant clusters, short syllables, voiced-stop endings — works on ANY language
- Semantic-tag filter (--grim): include only morphemes tagged grim/mortuary/monstrous/battle — works on ANY language

These two filters can apply to Slavic, OE, Latin, Welsh, etc. independently of the language's 'native' register. So a GM gets:
  --style slavic-east --everyday      → ordinary Russian-style village names
  --style slavic-east --harsh --grim  → menacing Russian-style fortress
  --style old-english --harsh --grim  → menacing Saxon-style fortress
  --style norman --everyday           → ordinary Norman village
  --style norman --harsh --grim       → menacing Norman keep

Each combination is legitimate. No language is pre-coded as the bad-guy register.

title: Dutch / Afrikaans register: mercantile-cities + colonial-frontier flavor
description:
Add Dutch and Afrikaans as fantasy registers for niches the British-isles palette doesn't cover well: mercantile city-states (Hanseatic-fantasy, Waterdeep-style canal cities), low-country wetlands, and colonial-frontier settings.

NOT a major densifier for existing British-isles consensus — Dutch's direct impact on English place naming is small (East Anglia fenland settlements, William III's nobility post-1689). The richer toponymic veins are in former Dutch-colonized regions: New Netherland (NY/NJ), South Africa (Afrikaans), Suriname.

Distinctive markers that read as Dutch to English ears:
- Suffixes: -dam, -haven, -poort, -werp, -dijk, -meer, -laan, -burgh
- Afrikaans suffixes: -fontein, -bosch, -veld, -kraal, -stad, -berg
- Phonemes: oe (/uː/), ij (/ɛi/), ui (/œy/), sch- (/sx/), throat-g (/ɣ/), doubled-vowel length

Fantasy register payoffs:
- 'Hanseatic merchant city-state' setting (think a Tolkien-ier version of D&D's Sword Coast): canal cities, trade leagues, merchant princes. Dutch is THE language for this.
- 'Trekker frontier' setting: Afrikaans-flavored. Hard land, settler outposts, distinctive from European-noble or English-pastoral. -fontein and -berg-driven.
- 'Low-country wetlands' with rich water-management vocabulary (polder, sluis, boezem, dijk, waard).

PD source coverage:
- Dutch proper: Johan Winkler (1837-1916), Verwijs & Verdam Middelnederlandsch Woordenboek (late 1800s), G.J. Boekenoogen dialectology (early 1900s)
- Afrikaans: sparser PD coverage, most compilations are mid-20th-c. Could lean on Dutch sources + a small set of distinctive Afrikaans markers seeded by hand.
- New Netherland (NY) toponymy: various NY historical society publications, late-1800s, PD

Language tags: 'dutch' (proper), 'afrikaans' (post-Cape derivation, where distinct).

Lower priority than the British-isles densification work since the consensus uplift is small, but a useful future register for fantasy worldbuilding diversity.

title: Mining: Nahuatl place-name corpus (separate from Mayan)
description:
Nahuatl is Uto-Aztecan, completely separate from Mayan. Different phonology, different morphology, different fantasy feel.

Distinctive Nahuatl markers:
- -tl lateral affricate suffix (Tenochtitlan, Tlaxcala, Cuauhnahuac, Quetzalcoatl) — iconic and untranslatable
- -tzin / -tzintli reverential
- Hu- representing /w/ (Huitzilopochtli, Cuauhtemoc, Tehuacán)
- -co / -tlan locative suffixes (Mexico = 'place of the Mexica')
- X = /ʃ/ (Xochimilco, Xochicalco — shared with Mayan orthographically only)
- 'Coatl' (serpent), 'tepec' (hill), 'mil' (cornfield), 'atl' (water) — high-frequency morphemes

PD sources to mine:
- Frederick Starr, 'Aztec Place-Names' (1920) — already found in our archive.org search
- Cecilio Robelo, 'Toponimia mexicana' (late 1800s)
- Antonio Peñafiel — foundational Mexican toponymy
- Nellie Sanchez, 'Spanish and Indian place names of California' (1914) — covers Nahuatl-derived California names

Fantasy register payoff: imperial sun-cult civilizations, stepped pyramids (different feel than Mayan), feathered-serpent gods, the 'Aztec' aesthetic of D&D's Maztica setting. Distinct from Mayan in feel.

Language code: nahuatl. Parent tag: mesoamerican (groups with mayan for setting-wide filters).
notes: Per user clarification: Nahuatl IS included in the bundleable set. Same as Mayan (wyrd-4qt) — Mesoamerican classical-empire frame, ancient-civilization documentation, no living-sovereignty-stake. Mine and bundle as a morally-neutral palette option. The 'dark/orcish' coding decision is REMOVED — Nahuatl is just Nahuatl, equally available for noble heroes, common villages, menacing antagonists, etc.

title: Mining: Mayan place-name corpus (separate from Nahuatl)
description:
Mayan and Nahuatl (Aztec) are completely different language families and need separate language tags. Mayan = Mayan family (Yucatec, K'iche', Q'eqchi', Tzotzil, etc.); Nahuatl = Uto-Aztecan. The X = /ʃ/ phoneme spelling is a shared colonial-Spanish orthography quirk, not a linguistic cognate.

Distinctive Mayan markers for fantasy register:
- X- prefix (Xunantunich, Xpujil, Xtubentun, X'cambo, Xelha) — visually iconic
- Yax- 'green/new/precious'
- Chac- 'great' / rain god
- K'in- 'sun, day'
- Itz- 'water/sorcerer' (Itzamná, Chichén Itzá)
- Tz affricate (Tzotzil)
- Glottal stops marked by apostrophe (K'iche', Q'eqchi')
- Long vowel marks (Maaya, Naachtun)

PD sources to mine:
- Diego de Landa, 'Relación de las cosas de Yucatán' (1566) — the foundational source, very PD
- Daniel Brinton, multiple Mayan works (late 1800s)
- Eduard Seler, German-language Mayan corpus (pre-1929 portions PD)
- Bishop Brasseur de Bourbourg, Popol Vuh translation + commentary (mid-1800s)
- Possibly William Gates 1920s

Suggested language codes:
- mayan-yucatec   (best documented; Landa, Brinton)
- mayan-kiche     (Popol Vuh, Brasseur)
- mayan-tzeltalan (sparser)
- mayan-cholan    (sparser)
Aggregate parent: mayan-family for tag-filtering.

Fantasy register payoff: ancient jungle civilizations, stepped pyramids, calendar/glyph magic, jaguar cults — a register that no European-language source can produce. Distinctive enough to be its own thing in the --style preset list (--style mayan, --style mesoamerican-mayan, etc.).
notes: Per user clarification: Mayan IS included in the bundleable set. The cultural-sensitivity caution applied to Native American / Aboriginal / Maori (active living communities with sovereignty/revitalization stakes), NOT to Mesoamerican classical-empire material. Mine and bundle without 'dark/exotic/villain' pre-coding — Mayan is just Mayan, equal palette option to OE or Latin.

title: Non-European place-name corpora: mining + sensitivity policy
description:
Extend the lexicon beyond the British Isles to give GMs distinctly non-European registers. Same schema/tooling as the British-isles work — only new language tags and source rows. Big quality-of-life lift for fantasy worldbuilding (Mesoamerican empires, Polynesian island chains, savanna kingdoms, etc.).

PHASE 1 — Bundleable PD sources (low cultural-sensitivity friction):

a) Mesoamerican (Nahuatl, Mayan via colonial Spanish):
   - Frederick Starr, 'Aztec Place-Names: Their Meaning and Mode of Composition' (1920) — found in our earlier archive.org search; not yet downloaded
   - Cecilio A. Robelo, 'Toponimia mexicana' — late 1800s, PD
   - Antonio Peñafiel — foundational Mexican toponymy, PD era

b) Latin American / colonial Spanish:
   - Nellie Sanchez, 'Spanish and Indian Place Names of California' (1914 / 1922) — also found in the search
   - Various Spanish-language colonial gazetteers (San Francisco, Santa Fe trail, etc.)

c) Algonquian / Iroquoian (US):
   - William Tooker, 'The Indian Place-Names on Long Island' (1911)
   - William Beauchamp, 'Aboriginal Place Names of New York' (1907)
   - Henry Schoolcraft (mid-1800s, very PD; pan-Algonquian)

d) Maori-Polynesian:
   - Edward Tregear, 'The Maori-Polynesian Comparative Dictionary' (1891) — PD, comprehensive

e) Bantu (limited but real):
   - Carl Meinhof, comparative Bantu phonology (early 1900s, PD)

PHASE 2 — Sensitivity-deferred (NOT bundled, framework-only):

For Indigenous languages with living speakers and active revitalization, do NOT bundle. Instead:
- Provide the language-pack format (wyrd-lcu) as the supported integration path
- Document: 'For Maori, Aboriginal Australian, Khoisan, etc. registers, contact community sources or use existing learning resources to build a pack respectfully'
- Add a content-warning note in the bundled-sources docs explaining why these aren't included by default

The PD-1907-1920 Algonquian/Iroquoian works are a borderline case. They're factually PD; the methodology was colonial. Compromise:
- Bundle them with explicit provenance notes ('compiled by William Tooker, 1911; for current respectful usage defer to tribal authorities')
- Tag those etymons with a 'historical-source' flag so GMs can choose to include or exclude them
- Default to NOT enabled in the standard fantasy-naming presets; require opt-in

CULTURAL-SENSITIVITY CONCERNS (worth documenting in the README):
1. Names of real sacred or living sites should not become fantasy random-generation output. The mining process should flag any toponym that's the actual name of a documented sacred/community site.
2. Generic morpheme inventories ('river', 'hill', 'place-of') are linguistically extractable but downstream users should know the source.
3. The bundled corpus is biased by who got to write the books in 1900-1925, which is mostly colonizers. Acknowledged limitation.

PHASE 3 — Fantasy register payoff:
  --style mesoamerican  → Nahuatl/Spanish for jungle empire / sun-cult settings
  --style latin-american → Spanish for mission frontier worlds
  --style polynesian → Tregear-derived for island chains
  --style savanna → Bantu-derived for African-flavored kingdoms

All using the same lexicon + composition machinery. Adds maybe 15-20K new etymons total to the corpus.
notes:
SPLIT: Mayan and Nahuatl are completely different language families. Filing as separate tickets with their own source corpora. This ticket now serves as the umbrella + sensitivity-policy / framework piece; the actual mining is in wyrd-{mayan} and wyrd-{nahuatl}.
REFRAMED — The sensitivity heuristic is sharper than 'non-European':

INCLUDE AND BUNDLE (morally-neutral palette options, no role-coding):
- Mesoamerican (Mayan wyrd-4qt, Nahuatl wyrd-f5h)
- Egyptian / Coptic
- Sumerian / Akkadian
- Ancient Greek / Latin (already done in wyrd-tqj/deq)
- Living-but-historically-broad (Arabic, Hebrew biblical-strata, Persian, Chinese, Japanese, large Bantu)

FRAMEWORK ONLY — don't bundle, provide language-pack format (wyrd-lcu) for community-supplied data:
- Native American (US/Canadian First Nations) — active sovereignty/revitalization
- Aboriginal Australian — same
- Maori, Hawaiian — same
- Khoisan — critically endangered, extreme sensitivity

The line is 'active living community with sovereignty/revitalization stake' vs 'classical/ancient civilization frame.' Not perfect (Hebrew straddles; Bantu varies), but a workable starting policy.

Bundled languages get morally-neutral treatment: Mayan can be the heroes' culture, Nahuatl can be the noble culture, etc. The user/GM decides at use time, not the engine. Same posture as for European languages in wyrd-xk9.

title: Orc/darklands register: grim semantic tags + harsh phonology + substrate
description:
A 'dark register' for fantasy worldbuilding (orcs, dread places, ancient ruins, forgotten tongues). Buildable largely from data we already have, with three layered components.

LAYER 1: Semantic tagging pass on existing etymons.
Add tags to relevant rows: 'grim', 'monstrous', 'mortuary', 'battle', 'wilderness', 'liminal'. Real OE/ON morphemes that fit:
- OE: wælstōw, morþor, bana, hræfn, draca, þorn, wulf, helle, wærg, mōr, fenn
- ON: draugr, nykr, troll, jǫtunn, vargr
- Already-mined: many of these are in the lexicon, just untagged

LAYER 2: Phonological-skew filter (--harsh).
Per-language preference-set: short syllables (1-2), voiced-stop endings, harsh consonant clusters (gr/kr/br/þ/ng/kk), reject vowel-final. Applied to ANY language's morphemes, produces the subset that sounds menacing. Doesn't pick a 'real ethnic group as the orc-language' — addresses the legitimate concern with Tolkien-esque coding of menace onto real cultures.

LAYER 3: Pre-Celtic substrate + Pictish overlay.
- Substrate: place names in Britain that don't fit Celtic/OE/Norse and are believed to descend from a lost pre-Indo-European / Old European language. River names mostly (Thames, Itchen, Severn, Avon, Humber). Scholars don't know what they meant.
- Pictish: poorly-understood language of pre-Gaelic Scotland, mostly attested through place-name elements (pit-, aber- with distinct distributions).
- Both strata are LITERALLY 'lost ancient tongues' — perfect for forgotten ruins, deep places, things predating human reckoning. Watson 1926 (already in sources/) covers these for Scotland; Lindkvist 1912 and Ekwall 1922 mention English substrate.

Mining target: explicitly mark substrate / pre-Celtic / Pictish entries with their own language code ('substrate' or 'pre-celtic') so they can be filtered.

Generation:
  --style orcish     → harsh phonology + grim semantic tags
  --style darkland   → substrate / pictish / lost-tongue subset
  --style ruin       → grim + harsh + ancient era

Pairs with wyrd-4lw (style presets) and wyrd-c1n (region+era lane). The dark register is a layering of existing primitives, not a new schema.

title: Bedrock provider for user-facing runtime LLM features
description:
Wire AWS Bedrock as a third --provider option (alongside ollama, gemini) for the LLM extractor, then use it from the lambda runtime to power interactive 'deluxe' features users couldn't get from precomputed data alone.

Architecture split:
- Ollama (local): bulk mining (~5000 entries × 5s, runs overnight, free)
- Gemini (cloud): review pass on questionable extractions (~140 entries × 10s per book, ~$1 each)
- Bedrock (cloud, intra-AWS): user-facing runtime features (per-request, billed via AWS)

Why Bedrock specifically:
- Already in AWS — same account as the lambda, IAM-based access (no API key shuffling)
- Anthropic's Claude is first-class on Bedrock — best quality model for this kind of nuanced linguistic / cultural reasoning
- Low latency intra-AWS
- AWS billing handles cost

Implementation: bedrock_extractor.py mirrors gemini_extractor.py:
- BedrockClient with model (default 'anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6')
- chat_json(system, user, schema) using bedrock-runtime InvokeModel API
- extract_one(client, ...) with same signature
- Validation guard reused from llm_extractor

Lambda runtime features this enables:
1. 'Explain in detail' — paragraph-of-prose enrichment beyond morpheme breakdown
2. 'Live homebrew translation' — user-typed deity / pinned name converted across registers on the fly
3. 'Cultural commentary' on cross-register output (what does each rendering FEEL like)
4. 'Generate variations around this seed' — given a place name, produce 5 similar
5. 'In-fiction description' for any generated name

Cost / rate-limit hygiene:
- Cache by (input-hash, feature) — repeat requests are free
- Per-IP rate limit at the API gateway
- Lambda has a request-budget cap so a malformed loop can't run away
- Fall back to precomputed data + 'enhanced description unavailable' if Bedrock errors

Lambda IAM addition: grant 'bedrock:InvokeModel' to the lambda's execution role for the specific Claude model ARN. No global Bedrock access.

title: Shavian transliterator: standalone text → Shavian generator
description:
A separate generator (wyrd/generators/shavian/) that takes arbitrary English text and outputs Shavian. Distinct from wyrd-y10 (which is about rendering individual generated place names in scripts) — this is a general-purpose text utility for whole prose, letters, prophecies, map legends, ritual texts, etc.

Core pipeline:
1. Tokenize input (preserve punctuation and whitespace).
2. For each word, look up in Read Lex (the 30K-word English-Shavian dictionary, openly available on GitHub).
3. For unknowns, fall back to G2P (grapheme-to-phoneme) via:
   - phonemizer library (calls espeak)
   - or g2p-en (pure-python, smaller install)
   - or rules-based (acceptable but lossy)
4. Apply Shavian conventions: namer dot for proper nouns, no capitalization, punctuation preserved.
5. Optional reverse direction: Shavian → English for round-trip verification by the GM.

Why this fits wyrd's architecture: wyrd's plugin framework already supports generic 'input → transform → output' generators. The Kenning generator does it for place names. A Shavian generator would do it for arbitrary text, register the same way (subclass Generator, define input_schema, generate), and the SPA picks it up automatically from the manifest.

Output formatting:
- Plain text (Unicode Shavian glyphs)
- HTML snippet with appropriate font-family hints (Noto Sans Shavian)
- Optional SVG export for handout-ready images
- Optional preserve-formatting mode (inputs with markdown / paragraph breaks come out in matching layout)

Family extension once shipped: Tengwar transliterator (with mode selector for English / Quenya / Sindarin), Elder Futhark, Ogham, Theban, etc. Each is its own generator, same plumbing.

Standalone use case validates this is worth its own generator vs. just being a kenning sub-feature: GMs who never touch the place-name tool would still use a Shavian transliterator for handouts.

title: Render names in alternate scripts (Shavian, Tengwar, Elder Futhark, etc.)
description:
Once the pronunciation pipeline (wyrd-17t) is in place, exposing names in alternate scripts is a small, additive feature with high tabletop value: GM produces handouts that LOOK foreign but can be decoded by interested players.

The brilliance of this for fantasy gaming: a phonemic script written for English IS English, just visually disguised. A player who learned Shavian can READ a 'foreign inscription' as plain English; a player who didn't sees mysterious glyphs. That's the perfect intersection of 'exotic enough to be atmospheric' and 'literally readable if you commit'.

Initial target: Shavian.
- Phonemic alphabet, ~48 letters, Unicode U+10450-U+1047F
- Maps to English phonemes 1:1 (so 'knight' → /naɪt/ → three glyphs)
- Read Lex (30K-word English-to-Shavian dictionary, openly available on GitHub) is the obvious data source
- Font: Noto Sans Shavian or Andagii — install instructions in docs

Family of follow-up scripts (each is just a phoneme→glyph table once Shavian's plumbing is in):
- Tengwar (Tolkien's elven; phoneme-based, multiple 'modes' per language)
- Cirth (Tolkien's runes; letter-mapped, simpler)
- Elder Futhark (real historical Germanic runes; fits norse/dwarvish coding)
- Ogham (real Irish stick-script; fits celtic/elven coding)
- Phoenician / Old Italic / Theban / Enochian (variously: ancient-empire, magical)

CLI shape:
  wyrd kenning generate --style elven --pin Claire --script tengwar
  wyrd kenning render 'Saint-Claire' --script shavian
  wyrd kenning render 'Hædan-tūn' --script elder-futhark

Output for handouts: ideally a small image or HTML snippet so the GM can paste it into a document. SVG with embedded font for portability.

Pairs with wyrd-17t (pronunciation) and wyrd-q5v (per-language composition patterns). Together they let the engine produce:
  Saint-Claire    /sant-KLAIR/   (modern, French-flavored)
  𐑕𐑲𐑯𐑑 𐑒𐑤𐑺  (Shavian rendering of same)
  saiŋt klar (Tengwar mode-of-English; visually elegant)
  ᛋᛇᚾᛏ ᚲᛚᚨᚱ (Elder Futhark, dwarvish-flavored)
All from one name, all phonologically derived from one underlying record.

title: Pluggable language-pack format for user-supplied lexicons
description:
Define a YAML/JSON schema for users to drop in their own language data and have it work with all the cross-register / pinning / generation tooling. Same approach as wyrd-g4a's pantheon plugin model.

Use cases this enables (without us shipping any of it):
- Tolkien's Middle-earth (Quenya, Sindarin, Adûnaic, Khuzdul) — Eldamo's data is structurally compatible; users with strong fan corpora can convert.
- Earthsea (Hardic, Old Speech, Kargish from Le Guin)
- Dragonlance, Forgotten Realms, Eberron in-setting languages
- D&D's Common/Elvish/Dwarvish/Draconic/Sylvan/etc.
- Any homebrew constructed language a worldbuilder has been refining for years.

Schema (mirrors our internal tables):
  language: <id>
  display_name: <human label>
  parent: <e.g. 'celtic-brittonic'>  # optional, inherits phonology rules
  phonology: { grapheme: <ipa>, ... }  # for pronunciation derivation
  inflection_rules: { suffix: label, ... }  # like our INFLECTION_RULES
  composition_patterns: [...]  # how compounds are built in this language
  etymons:
    - canonical_form: <form>
      gloss: [<meaning>, ...]
      tags: [topographical, personal-name, ...]
      modifier_type: <topo|habitative|...>
      lemma_of: <id of related lemma if inflected>
      inflection: <if inflected>

Users drop the YAML at ~/.wyrd/language-packs/<name>.yaml and a CLI command imports it into a per-user lexicon overlay. Generation can target the user's pack the same way it targets bundled languages (--style sindarin --era third-age).

Licensing posture: we ship NO Tolkien/Paizo/WotC content. Users supply their own under whatever fair use / personal use applies to them. Community can share packs informally; we provide tooling and don't host content.

Pairs with wyrd-g4a (homebrew pantheons), wyrd-nd2 (etymon pools), and wyrd-q5v (composition patterns) — all share the 'user-defined data feeds the same engine' design.

title: GM-controlled etymon pool for region-flavored generation
description:
Let a GM say 'in this region, names should be built from these specific morphemes' and the generator constrains itself to that pool. The data model already supports this (etymons are first-class rows); we just need the UX.

Use cases:
- 'This region is the Wolfmoor: every place-name should draw from morphemes meaning wolf, hill, blood, mist, fire, oak.' GM provides a list of glosses or specific etymon ids; generator filters.
- 'My homebrew elves are Welsh-flavored but with these specific personal names: Aelwyn, Caradoc, Maelgwn, Tegwen.' GM provides personal-name etymons; generator uses them in compositions.
- 'For this dwarven hold, only use morphemes that appear in Mawer\'s Northumberland-Durham corpus' (a region-locked vocabulary).

Implementation:
- Generator gains --etymon flags (repeatable) or --etymon-pool <yaml>
- A pool can be specified by:
  - Specific etymon ids (most precise)
  - Gloss filter ('any etymon meaning wolf or hill')
  - Source filter ('only etymons cited by source X')
  - Tag filter ('any etymon tagged forest, religion, or animal')
- Combinable with --style and --era so the GM can layer 'elven register, ancient era, but only these specific words'.

Companion to wyrd-g4a (pantheons): a GM's deity table and word pool together define the naming flavor of a setting. Combined output: 'Tref-Mistwen on the slopes of Coed-Aelwyn' produced from a few constraints rather than randomly across the whole corpus.
notes:
Add 'pinned name' feature. A GM should be able to pin a specific name string into generation and have the system either (a) inflect it for the target register, or (b) treat it as an intact chunk to decorate around.

Two modes (auto-detected from input shape):

Mode 1 — Single token, attempt conjugation:
  --pin Claire
  → modern: 'Saint Claire'
  → latin: 'Sancta Clarae' (genitive feminine 1st declension)
  → french: 'Saint-Cler' (Norman shortening)
  → welsh: 'Llan-Glair' (with appropriate soft mutation)
  → OE: 'Clairan' (weak feminine genitive, conjugated by inflection rules)
  → norse: 'Klare-' (transliterated to Norse phonology, no native cognate)

Mode 2 — Phrase / hyphenated compound, treat as chunk:
  --pin Saint-Claire
  → modern: 'Saint-Claire Manor'
  → french: 'Saint-Claire-en-les-Champs'
  → norse: 'Klare-stad' (transliterated chunk + Norse topographical element)
  System only varies the connector + the topographical element, never breaks the pinned phrase.

Auto-detection rule: if the input contains a hyphen or a known honorific prefix (Saint, Lord, King) → mode 2; otherwise mode 1.

Cross-register transliteration when no cognate exists:
- For Norse/Welsh/Brittonic, when the pinned name has no native equivalent, fall back to phonological transliteration following the target language's rules. Mark the result is_native=false in the output so the GM knows it's a constructed adaptation, not an attested name.
- This pairs with wyrd-17t (pronunciation) — the same per-language phonology table feeds both directions.

CLI shape:
  wyrd kenning generate --style elven --pin Claire
  wyrd kenning generate --era ancient --pin Saint-Claire
  wyrd kenning generate --pin Aldric    # pin a king's name in modern register
  wyrd kenning generate --pin Maelaria --to elven,latin,norse  # show all renderings

title: Pantheon table + cross-register deity rendering
description:
Add a deity layer so the generator can produce place names anchored to specific TTRPG pantheons (Pathfinder Sarenrae, D&D Lathander, etc.) AND render those deity names in any cultural register. Precomputed table — no runtime LLM calls required.

Schema:
  pantheon              (id, name, description)
  deity                 (id, pantheon_id, canonical_name, gender, alignment, description)
  deity_domain          (deity_id, domain)  -- sun, healing, fire, redemption
  deity_render          (deity_id, register, rendered_name, is_authentic, confidence, notes)
  deity_render_etymon   (deity_id, register, etymon_id)
    -- links the rendered name back into the etymology graph so place
    -- generation treats it as a personal-name etymon

Use cases:
- 'Generate a saint-cult village dedicated to Sarenrae, in elven register'
  → Llan-Heulwen / Tref-Heulwen (Welsh for 'sun-blessing village')
- 'Same town, render across the registers'
  → modern: Sarenrae's Vale; saxon: Sunngifu-dene; norse: Sólgyða-dalr; latin: Vallis Solinae

IP / licensing:
- Ship with public-domain pantheons only (Norse, Greek, Roman, Celtic, Egyptian, Mesopotamian, etc.) — these are real religion and out of copyright.
- Game-specific pantheons (Pathfinder, D&D, Eberron, Forgotten Realms) live as user-supplied data files in ~/.wyrd/pantheons/<id>.yaml. We provide a JSON schema and a CLI to validate/import them, but don't bundle any commercial pantheons in the repo.
- Homebrew pantheons same path: write the YAML, drop it in.

Render-table population:
- One-shot LLM batch with human review, results checked into the repo for the bundled (PD) pantheons.
- For user-added pantheons: 'wyrd kenning render-deity <name> --domains <list>' calls Gemini once, caches results to the user's local data dir.

Cross-register mapping is artistic not linguistic — the LLM is doing 'name a sun-and-healing goddess in Welsh phonology that fits the vibe', not translating. Mark synthesized names with is_authentic=0 so GMs can tell which renderings are real attested names from the target tradition vs. constructed-to-fit.
notes:
Adding native_register concept. Many designed pantheons (Pathfinder especially) phoneme-code their deities to a real-world register: Sarenrae/Iomedae are Latin (-ae feminine), Asmodeus/Pharasma are Greek (-eus, -asma), Cayden Cailean has a real Gaelic second name, etc. Paizo did this on purpose at the phoneme level.

Schema addition:
  deity.native_register TEXT  -- the register the canonical name already reads as

Implications:
- Rendering 'to native register' is identity (Sarenrae → Sarenrae in Latin context).
- Rendering 'to another register' is the substantive cross-cultural conversion.
- We can INFER native_register from the canonical name's phoneme profile (endswith -ae/-us → latin; -dd/-ll/-wy → welsh; -r after consonant cluster → norse). That spares users from having to declare it for homebrew deities.

Also: when adding a homebrew deity via CLI, the inference + 'is this right?' confirmation step is a nice UX.
License stance update: don't ship-block on this. At worst, if a publisher gets pissy we substitute descriptive names ('D&D god of war' instead of 'Tempus') while keeping all the cross-register renderings intact. Real risk is low because we're using deity names as references for naming logic, not reproducing setting fluff or stat blocks.

Add: a 'translate-deity' tool for HOMEBREW gods. GM declares 'my goddess Mistweaver, domains: forest, dream, illusion, female'; the tool runs the same render-deity flow used for bundled pantheons, producing per-register variants. CLI like:

  wyrd kenning translate-deity 'Mistweaver' \
    --domains forest,dream,illusion --gender female \
    --to elven,saxon,norse,latin

The output is a YAML the GM can drop into ~/.wyrd/pantheons/<world>.yaml and use thereafter. Same machinery as for bundled pantheons; just on-demand for homebrew. This is probably MORE important than the bundled pantheons since serious GMs run homebrew worlds.

title: Pronunciation guide for non-modern-English outputs
description:
When the generator produces names like Brycgwæter, Pont-Dwfr, Brúarvatn, English-speaking users can't sound them out. We need a respelling alongside the canonical form so they're usable at the table.

Two sources:

1. SCHOLAR-ATTESTED pronunciation, mined from the etymology books. Mawer 1920 writes phonetic transcriptions in square brackets for many entries: 'Acomb [ækəm] (Bywell St Peter)...'. The dictionary parser already strips these out; capture the bracket contents on ingest. Add 'phonetic' column to toponym (or a separate toponym_phonetic table for multiple-system support — IPA vs respelling). Same likely doable for some Skeat and Watson entries.

2. RULE-DERIVED pronunciation for generated/invented names. Per-language grapheme-to-phonetic-respelling tables:
   - Old English (æ, ð, þ, cg, sc, palatalized c, long-vowel marks)
   - Welsh (dd, ll, f, ff, w-as-vowel, y)
   - Old Norse (þ, ð, j, á/ó/ú)
   - Norman French (silent endings, é, ç, vowel rules)
   - Latin (largely transparent to English readers; mark long vowels and stress)
   - Greek (transliterated forms; ph→f, ch→k, kh→k)

Display layout for end users:
   Pont-Dwfr   /pont DOO-ver/   'bridge of water' (elven, Welsh)

Three lines: form, respelling, gloss + register tag. Optional IPA on a verbose flag for linguistically interested users.

Stress and syllable boundaries: mark stress with capitals on the stressed syllable, separate syllables with hyphens. SAMPA-lite respelling (BRIDGE-wuh-tər, BROO-ar-vatn) is more accessible than IPA and good enough for the table.

title: Register conversion: render the same name across cultural registers
description:
Take a place name (real or invented) and re-render it in a different language/cultural register, preserving meaning. Bridgwater → Pont-d'Aigue (noble) → Brúarvatn (dwarvish) → Pons Aquae (imperial), all from the same etymological backbone.

Mechanism (uses existing schema):
1. Decompose the input via the explainer (already exists).
2. For each element, look up its gloss(es) in etymon_gloss.
3. For each gloss, find an etymon in the TARGET language with that gloss (or a near-neighbor gloss if exact match missing).
4. Apply the target language's compound pattern (wyrd-tk1 'per-language composition patterns') + inflection rules (wyrd-8ho).
5. Emit the result, optionally with a 'gloss coverage report' showing which elements translated cleanly vs. fell back.

Failure mode to handle: not every gloss has a clean cross-language equivalent. OE 'burh' → Latin 'castrum' is solid; OE 'thwaite' (clearing) → Welsh has no direct word. When no match: report the gap and offer the nearest neighbor with a confidence note.

CLI shape (illustrative):
  wyrd kenning convert 'Bridgwater' --to noble
  wyrd kenning convert 'Bridgwater' --tour    # all registers at once

Pairs naturally with --style for fresh generation. A 'tour' display showing one place across 7 cultural lenses is probably the killer demo for this whole engine — it directly shows what the lemma+gloss data layer enables.

title: Fantasy race / culture style presets in the generator
description:
Tolkien-style mapping of cultural register → fantasy race-coding. The data already supports filtering by language and era; this is the user-facing sugar.

Defaults (subject to taste):
- elven   → celtic (with a sub-toggle for brittonic vs goidelic vs cornish)
- dwarven → old-norse OR old-english (sub-toggle, or 'germanic-dwarven' for both)
- saxon   → old-english (modernized)
- imperial → latin
- mythic  → greek
- norman  → norman-french
- modern  → modern-english (default)

Pairs naturally with --era for time-stratification:
  --style elven --era ancient   → fully OE/Brittonic, no modernization
  --style elven --era weathered → middle-period, partly worn-down
  --style elven --era modern    → fully modernized (less likely use case)

Implementation: a STYLE_PRESETS table in cli.py that maps preset name → (language, modifier-type-bias, optional sub-toggles). Generator gains  option that applies the filter alongside --era. Fully derivable from existing data once language/era axes are in place.

This is the feature most users will actually use — 'give me elven city names', not 'give me names with celtic morphemes from 600-1000 AD'. Both routes available.
notes:
Add explicit Norman-French handling. To the English-speaking reader, Norman-French names code as 'foreign hostile court / aristocratic villainy' specifically — different from Latin's 'old institutional / dead empire' coding. The whole genre exploits this gradient (Lannister, Lestrange, Malfoy, Bellatrix, Sheriff of Nottingham vs Robin of Locksley). Useful presets:

- 'noble' / 'aristocrat' / 'villainous': norman-french with Beau-/Bel-/Mal- bias
- 'high-court': norman-french for surnames + latin for institutional names

Reminder: Zachrisson 1909 (already in sources/) is specifically about Anglo-Norman influence on English place names — high-priority mining target to fill out this register since it's currently underrepresented (~56 etymons, mostly from rando-port).

title: Per-language composition patterns for cross-cultural rendering
description:
With lemma_id + inflection now in place (wyrd-8ho), the generator has the morphological pieces to compose names, but it doesn't yet know the SHAPE of compounds in each language.

Old English: genitive personal name + topographical noun (Hædan-tūn).
Old Norse: genitive personal name + topographical noun (Hægna-býr) — structurally similar to OE.
Welsh: topographical noun + (genitive) personal name, with mutation (Llan-Mair).
Latin: domus/villa + genitive (Villa Sancti Petri).
French: saint name connected by hyphen / 'de' particle (Saint-Pierre-en-Hayes).

Each language has its own compositional template AND its own connector tokens / particles / mutations. The inflection table tells us how to inflect a given lemma for a given role; the missing piece is the structural pattern that says 'in this language, a Habitative compound has slots [genitive_personal_name, topographical_lemma]'.

Required to ship cross-cultural rendering (wyrd-sfp). Probably:
- New table 'name_pattern' (language, modifier_type combo, slot list, connector tokens).
- Per-pattern rendering function in generator that fills slots.
- Per-language phonological glue (e.g. Welsh initial mutation, OE assimilation).

Nice property: data layer (etymons + inflections) is shared across all languages; only the patterns and glue rules are per-language. That's the right separation.

title: Dictionary parser captures sentence fragments in Mawer
description:
Mawer's body sometimes has prose paragraphs that get OCR-split mid-sentence, producing 'paragraphs' starting with capitalized words like 'Self-explanatory', 'Burn', 'Hill', 'House', 'Beck', 'Law', 'PI'. Current entry-headword regex matches them as toponyms.

Fix: require the entry body to contain at least one validating signal — a 4-digit year, an 'O.E./A.S./O.N.' marker, or 'Phonology, §' — before accepting the heading as an entry. Real Mawer entries always have at least one of these; sentence fragments don't.

Lower priority since the noise is small (~7 spurious toponyms out of 386) but they show up in the disagreement view, which makes the review noisier than it should be.
close_reason: Fixed via dictionary_parser body-signal validator + extended false-headwords list. Mawer parser now produces 804 entries (down from 838), with all 7 known false positives filtered (Burn, Hill, House, Beck, Law, PI, Self-explanatory). Real entries (Abberwick, Acomb, Acklington, Aislaby) preserved. 2 new tests added.

title: Greek as a productive register parallel to Latin
description:
Same property as Latin (wyrd-deq) but with distinct compositional rules and stylistic feel. English absorbs enough Greek through scientific/scholarly vocabulary that morphemes like polis, akro, megalo, micro, oros, nesos, thalassa, potamos, -ia (Thessalia/Aetolia/Arcadia), -os (Argos/Mykos) are intuitively parseable as 'ancient/scholarly/mythic'.

Greek compositional rules differ from Latin:
- Direct stem-joining (akro+polis = Acropolis) is common, vs Latin's preference for noun + adjective (Mons Lupinus).
- Genders/declensions matter but slightly different.
- Loves -ia and -os endings for region/place names.

Stylistically distinct from Latin: Latin reads imperial/civic/military; Greek reads ancient/scholarly/mythic. Setting can use both without feeling redundant.

Source corpus: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography (already filed as wyrd-gxf — covers both languages). Deeper sources for later: Stephanus of Byzantium's Ethnika, Pape's Wörterbuch der griechischen Eigennamen (1850, German, PD).

title: Mine Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography for Latin place data
description: William Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography (1854) is public domain on archive.org, two large volumes. Covers nearly every named place in the Roman empire and Greek world with Latin/Greek forms and brief etymology. Ideal seed corpus for Latin morpheme inventory work — gives us productive examples (which morphemes appear in real attested Roman place names, in what proportions). Even though we're framing Latin as productive-not-attestation-based, the real Roman corpus tells us which morphemes are genuinely productive vs literary curios.

title: Latin as a productive register independent of attestation corpus
description:
Unlike Anglo-Saxon/Celtic/Norse layers (which need attested historical place names from Skeat-style corpora), Latin can be a 'productive register' — a morpheme inventory + compositional rules that mints names which feel Roman to an English reader regardless of whether they actually existed.

Required:
- Topographic morpheme inventory: castrum/castra, villa, vicus, mons, silva, aqua, forum, pons, portus, oppidum, etc. with positions (most Latin compounds are noun + adjective so 'pre-noun + post-adjective': Mons Lupinus, Aqua Sulis).
- Modifier vocabulary: magna/maxima, minor/parva, nova/novum, vetus, alta, bona, etc. with gender-agreement rules (since Latin agrees adjectives to nouns).
- Personal-name → estate suffixes: -ium, -ianum, -anum (Domus Petri, Villa Petriana).
- A 'register: latin' parameter that picks from this inventory and applies Latin grammatical rules (declension, gender agreement) at composition time.

Frees the project from being British-Isles-only — Latin becomes a cultural palette useful for fantasy worldbuilding anywhere.

title: Mine Domesday Book place-name index
description: Domesday Book (1086) is a unique moment-in-time snapshot of nearly every English settlement's name. Public-domain transcriptions exist (e.g. Phillimore edition). Each entry gives the Domesday spelling alongside its modern county/hundred — perfect feed for toponym_attestation rows dated 1086. Would dramatically densify the Anglo-Saxon period coverage.

title: Mine English Place-Name Society pre-1929 county surveys
description: EPNS started publishing county-by-county etymological surveys in 1923. The pre-1929 ones (Mawer/Stenton vol 1+2, Buckinghamshire 1925, etc.) are public domain in the US. Modern volumes (~90 by now) are still copyrighted but the early ones cover ~6 counties at higher rigor than Skeat. Worth mining as a layer above Skeat for cross-source consensus.

title: Stratified map generation: same region rendered at multiple eras
description: Generate two maps of the same region with period-consistent names: a Domesday map (Cestretone, Hædan-tūn) and a modern map (Chesterton, Haddenham) sharing identical underlying toponyms. Bulk-generate-and-render with region+era anchoring.

title: Region + era stylistic lane
description: Generator parameter constraining output to one region's typical morpheme inventory + one era's surface forms. 'Anglo-Saxon Mercia ~900 AD' samples only morphemes attested in that region in that period. Filter once region tags exist on toponyms and period axis is in.

title: Generator: name families sharing an etymon
description: Pick a personal name or topographic etymon and generate a cluster of related places: Hædan's manor (Hædan-tūn), Hædan's lake (Hædan-mere), Hædan's clearing (Hædan-lēah). The schema already supports this — bind one etymon, vary the other from compatible co-occurrence patterns. Add a generator mode 'family' with a seed etymon, returns N coherent compounds.

title: Time-rewind explainer: project a modern/invented name backward
description: Inverse of forward-generation. Player invents 'Springvale'; explainer answers 'pre-1700 this would have been Sprinc-feld'. Builds on the explainer feature plus the period-form infrastructure.

title: Cross-cultural rendering: same place, multiple cultures simultaneously
description: Render the same etymological frame in 2+ cultures: Hædan-tūn (Old English) / Hægni-býr (Old Norse) / Tre-Hayd (Welsh) / Haedenovilla (Latin). Killer test: Londinium → Lundenwic → Lunden → London crosses both time and culture axes.

title: Mine Holder's Alt-celtischer Sprachschatz for pre-Anglo-Saxon forms
